table.title: A virtual reality (VR) experiment on the effects of teacher praise
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
RQ: Does receiving praise from the teacher, while an equally performing classmate does not, lead children to perceive themselves as less smart but more hardworking?

H1: We hypothesize that receiving praise from the teacher while an equally performing classmate does not (vs. not receiving praise from the teacher while an equally performing classmate does), leads children to perceive themselves as less smart.

H2: We hypothesize that receiving praise from the teacher while an equally performing classmate does not (vs. not receiving praise from the teacher while an equally performing classmate does), leads children to perceive themselves as more hardworking.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Our study consists of two parts: a pre-experimental questionnaire and a Virtual Reality (VR) experiment. In the questionnaire, we will index predictors. In the VR experiment, we examine the effects of praise on dependent variables. Before the study, after providing consent, parents/caregivers will be asked to complete an optional questionnaire indexing the child’s background (e.g., socioeconomic status).

Our key dependent variables:
1. Self-perceived ability:
a) Who is smarter, do you think?  You or the other student? [dichotomous]
b) How much smarter are you/is the other student, do you think? [3-point scale]

2. Self-perceived effort:
a) Who worked harder on the task, do you think? You or the other student? [dichotomous]
b) How much harder did you/the other student work, do you think? (3-point scale)

In the items above, the word “task” will be replaced with “figuren-opdrachten” (i.e., the Dutch name of the task).

For self-perceived ability and self-perceived effort separately, participants’ responses will be transformed to a 6-point scale, ranging from 1 (classmate is much higher in self-perceived ability/effort) to 6 (participant is much higher in self-perceived ability/effort).
table.study_design_overview:
In the VR experiment, the participant will enter a virtual classroom with a virtual teacher and a virtual classmate. The participant and the virtual classmate both perform a task and achieve the same score. 

The participant will be randomly assigned, between subjects, to one of two conditions:
1. The self-praise condition: The participant receives praise, but the classmate does not
2. The other-praise condition: The classmate receives praise, but the participant does not
table.statistical_tests: We will run 2 regression analyses (i.e., one for each dependent variable), with experimental condition as a dichotomous independent variable. We will test each hypothesis at α = .05, two-tailed. H1 is confirmed if children in the self-praise condition report significantly lower self-perceived ability than do children in the other-praise condition. H2 is confirmed if children in the self-praise condition report significantly higher self-perceived effort than do children in the other-praise condition.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will exclude observations meeting one or more of the following four criteria:
1. The parent/caregiver or child withdrew their data from the study.
2. The child has fully missing data on all key dependent variables.
3. The experimenter misdelivered the praise in VR in a way that interferes with random assignment (i.e., the experimenter did not deliver teacher praise while they should have, or the experimenter delivered teacher praise while they should not have, to the participant or the virtual classmate).
4. Critical technical malfunctions (e.g., the computer or VR equipment failed and could not be restarted, leading to an abortion of the experiment before the child completed at least one key dependent variable).

We will not exclude outliers from our preregistered analyses. We will, however, rerun our preregistered analyses after excluding participants with a Cook’s distance exceeding 1.

If responses to individual items are missing (e.g., if a child accidentally skipped a question in the classroom questionnaire), we will average responses across items that they did complete.
table.sample_size:
We aim to test a minimum of 140 participants, including those who meet our exclusion criteria. We will continue to collect data up to and including June 30, 2024, even if we have already reached the 140 participants before this date, for two reasons. First, we seek to maximize statistical power. Second, several schools have already agreed to participate in our research, and we cannot estimate exactly how many children will end up participating. Thus, our final sample size might exceed our preregistered sample size. If we have reached 140 participants and have tested all eligible children in the participating schools before June 30, 2024, we will terminate data collection before June 30, 2024. We will include the full sample in our analyses. If, however, we have not reached 140 participants by June 30, 2024, we will continue to collect data (e.g., in the new school year) until we have reached 140 participants.

Master’s students will assist in data collection as part of their thesis projects. They will have to start analyzing data early May 2024. Thus, we will share with them data of the participants that have been tested up to and including April 29, 2024. If the number of participants exceeds 70 at this date, we will share with them the first 70 participants (including those who meet our exclusion criteria), without inspecting or analyzing data of the other participants. After sharing the data with the students, we will not inspect or analyze date of subsequent participants before terminating data collection.
table.additional_comments:
In addition to the key dependent variables, we will assess a series of variables:

A. CLASSROOM QUESTIONNAIRE:
1. Gender (boy, girl, or neither)
2. Age (6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, or 13 years)
3. Grade (Dutch group 5, 6, 7, or 8)
4. Subjective social status: MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status (1 item, 10-point scale; Adler et al., 2000; Amir et al., 2019)
5. Child-reported household possessions (14 items, with different types of response scales; based on Kastberg et al., 2021)
6. Self-perceived ability (3 items, 4-point scale)
7. Self-perceived effort (3 items, 4-point scale)
8. Uncertainty about teacher’s perceptions of one’s intelligence (3 items, 4-point scale)
9. Uncertainty about teacher’s liking of the self (3 items, 4-point scale)
10. Self-esteem: Lifespan Self-Esteem scale (4 items, 5-point scale; Harris et al., 2018)
11. Narcissism: Childhood Narcissism Scale (10 items, 4-point scale; Thomaes et al., 2008)
12. Mindset: Mindset Scale (6 items, 6-point scale; Dweck, 1999)

B. PARENT/CAREGIVER QUESTIONNAIRE:
1. Highest level of completed education of both parents/caregivers separately (Basisonderwijs, VMBO-b/k , VMBO-g/t, Onderbouw HAVO, Onderbouw VWO, MBO1, MBO2, MBO3, MBO4, HAVO, VWO, Bachelor HBO, Bachelor Universiteit, Master HBO, Master Universiteit, Doctorstitel; based on Schröder, 2014)
2. Migration status for both parents/caregivers and the child (1 item, 2-point scale: Born in the Netherlands yes/no? If no, in which country were/was you/the other parent/caregiver/child born?)

C. VR EXPERIMENT:
1. Challenge seeking (based on Brummelman et al., 2014; Mueller & Dweck, 1998). In the VR classroom, in four trials, children choose which tasks to do next: an easy task (scored as 0) or a difficult task (scored as 1). Their responses will be averaged.
2. Mindset about the task: Do you think you can get better at the task, if you really do your best? (1 item, 4-point scale)
3. Teacher-perceived ability:
a) Who does the teacher think is smarter, do you think? You or the other student? [dichotomous]
b) How much smarter does the teacher think you are/the other student is, do you think? [3-point scale]
4. Teacher-perceived effort:
a) Who does the teacher think worked harder on the task, do you think? You or the other student? [dichotomous]
b) How much harder does the teacher think you/the other student worked on the task? (3-point scale)
5. Teacher liking of the self:
a) Who does the teacher like better, do you think? You or the other student? [dichotomous]
b) How much better does the teacher like you/the other student, do you think? (3-point scale)

table.research_questions:
Our study includes four conditions:
1.	The self-praise condition: The participant receives praise, but the classmate does not
2.	The other-praise condition: The classmate receives praise, but the participant does not
3.	The both-praise condition: Both the participant and the classmate receive praise
4.	The neither-praise condition: Neither the participant nor the classmate receives praise

RQ1: Does receiving praise from the teacher, while an equally performing classmate does not, lead children to infer that the teacher thinks they are low in ability?

H1: We hypothesize that children in the self-praise condition report lower teacher-perceived ability than do children in the other-praise condition.

RQ2: Does receiving praise from the teacher, while an equally performing classmate does not, lead children to infer that they are low in ability?

H2: We hypothesize that children in the self-praise condition report lower self-perceived ability than do children in the other-praise condition.

RQ3: Does receiving praise from the teacher, while an equally performing classmate does not, lead children to experience low self-esteem?

H3: We hypothesize that children in the self-praise condition report lower state self-esteem than do children in the other-praise condition.

We included the both-praise and neither-praise conditions to explore whether the effects described in hypotheses 1, 2, and 3 are driven by receiving praise per se or by receiving praise while an equally performing classmate does not. Comparisons involving the both-praise and neither-praise conditions will be exploratory. 

We will assess children’s physiological responses (i.e., heart rate, skin conductance, blushing) to the interaction with the teacher. We will explore differences between conditions in these responses.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Our study consists of two parts: a pre-experimental questionnaire and a Virtual Reality (VR) experiment. In the pre-experimental questionnaire, we will index predictors. In the VR experiment, we will examine the effects of praise on dependent variables. While children complete the experiment, parents/caregivers complete a questionnaire indexing the child’s background (e.g., socioeconomic status) and additional variables. 

Our key dependent variables:

For each dependent variable, children report how they feel or what they think RIGHT NOW, AT THIS MOMENT.

Teacher-Perceived Ability (3 items, 4-point scale):
Teacher Anouk probably…
1. thinks that I am good at Memory
2. believes that I can do well in Memory
3. thinks that I have talent for Memory
 
Self-Perceived Ability (3 items, 4-point scale)
1. I think that I am good at Memory
2. I believe that I can do well in Memory
3. I think that I have talent for Memory

State Self-Esteem (4 items, 4-point scale):
1. I feel satisfied with myself
2. I feel bad about myself (reverse coded)
3. I feel unsatisfied with myself (reverse coded)
4. I feel good about myself

Responses will be averaged across items.
table.study_design_overview: In the VR experiment, the participant will enter a virtual classroom with a virtual teacher and a virtual classmate. The participant and the virtual classmate both perform memory tasks and achieve the same score. The participant will be randomly assigned, between subjects, to one of four conditions: (1) the self-praise condition, (2) the other-praise condition, (3) the both-praise condition, or (4) the neither-praise condition. The interaction will be repeated once (i.e., it will occur twice but each time with a different memory task, thus ensuring credibility).
table.statistical_tests:
We will run one ANOVA for each dependent variable. Experimental condition (self-praise, other-praise, both-praise, neither-praise) will serve as a between-subjects variable. Our hypotheses pertain to pairwise comparisons, regardless of the significance of the omnibus F-test. We will test our hypotheses at α = .05, two-tailed.

H1 is confirmed if teacher-perceived ability is lower in the self-praise condition than in the other-praise condition.
H2 is confirmed if self-perceived ability is lower in the self-praise condition than in the other-praise condition.
H3 is confirmed if state self-esteem is lower in the self-praise condition than in the other-praise condition.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Dutch-speaking children aged 8-13 years are eligible for participation.

We will exclude observations meeting one or more of the following four criteria:
1. The parent/caregiver or child withdrew their data from the study.
2. The child has fully missing data on all key dependent variables.
3. The experimenter misdelivered the praise in VR in a way that interferes with random assignment (i.e., the experimenter did not deliver teacher praise while they should have, or the experimenter delivered teacher praise while they should not have, to the participant or the virtual classmate).
4. Critical technical malfunctions (e.g., the computer or VR equipment failed and could not be restarted, leading to an abortion of the experiment before the child completed at least one key dependent variable).
5. The assessment was marked as a pilot by the experimenter before testing a participant. Experimenters may do a few pilots to make sure the procedure runs smoothly; they indicate whether a session is a pilot in the Qualtrics, prior to participation of the child.

We will not exclude outliers from our preregistered analyses. We will, however, rerun our preregistered analyses after excluding participants with a Cook’s distance exceeding 1.

If responses to individual items are missing (e.g., if a child accidentally skipped a question in the classroom questionnaire), we will average responses across items that they did complete.
table.sample_size:
We will conduct our study in a science museum. We are allowed a 16-day period of data collection (from October 19, 2024, up to and including November 3, 2024), and we will test as many participants as possible within that time period, so as to maximize statistical power for testing differences between the four experimental conditions.
 
We aim to test a minimum of 160 participants (excluding pilots but including those who meet our other exclusion criteria). We will continue to collect data up to and including November 3, 2024, even if we have already reached the 160 participants before this date. We will include the full sample in our analyses. If, however, we have not reached 160 participants by November 3, 2024, we will continue to collect data (e.g., in the next semester, at the museum or in schools) until we have reached this number.
 
We will inspect and analyze the data of the first 20 participants (including pilot participants) to see if there are any programming or procedural errors; we will not inspect or analyze data of subsequent participants. Thus, our decision to terminate data collection on November 3, 2024, cannot be influenced by our results.

text.text: We did not deviate from the preregistration, but we do report additional exploratory analyses.
An NWO Talent Programme Vidi Grant (VI.Vidi.211.181) and Jacobs Foundation Research Fellowship (2020-1362-02) awarded to Eddie Brummelman supported this research.
Teachers often praise students to make them feel smart (Brummelman, 2020; Henderlong & Lepper, 2002).
text.formatted: Teachers often praise students to make them feel smart <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brummelman, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Henderlong & Lepper, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: They dole out praise up to more than once per minute (Scott & and Tsai, 2025), often giving more praise to children from disadvantaged backgrounds (Harber, 2023; Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023).
text.formatted: They dole out praise up to more than once per minute <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Scott & and Tsai, 2025)</ref>, often giving more praise to children from disadvantaged backgrounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Harber, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: But praise may not always have the intended positive outcome.
Imagine two children receiving the same grade, and the teacher lavishing praise on only one: "Wow, you did a great job!"
Children know that teachers praise those who succeed through hard work rather than natural ability (Barker & Graham, 1987).
text.formatted: Children know that teachers praise those who succeed through hard work rather than natural ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barker & Graham, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, ironically, the praised student may infer that they are less smart.
Indeed, this is a concern that has been voiced in social, developmental, and educational psychology (Brummelman, 2020).
text.formatted: Indeed, this is a concern that has been voiced in social, developmental, and educational psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brummelman, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We tested this idea through two preregistered Virtual Reality (VR) experiments with 7-to 13-year-old children.
text.formatted: We tested this idea through two preregistered Virtual Reality <ref type="bibr">(VR)</ref> experiments with 7-to 13-year-old children.

text.text: Using virtual reality tools, we immersed children in a virtual classroom with virtual classmates and a virtual teacher, allowing us to isolate the causal effect of teacher praise in a dynamic social context.
Teachers treat students differentially to tailor their education to students' level of ability (Parsons et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Teachers treat students differentially to tailor their education to students' level of ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Parsons et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In some cases, however, teachers' views are influenced less by a student's individual characteristics and more by their background.

This may lead teachers to offer more negative feedback to students from disadvantaged backgrounds-for example, asking simpler questions, providing less sophisticated feedback, or assigning lower grades and track recommendations-thereby perpetuating inequality (Bloem et al., 2026; Brummelman et al., 2026; Brummelman & Sedikides, 2023; Turetsky et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This may lead teachers to offer more negative feedback to students from disadvantaged backgrounds-for example, asking simpler questions, providing less sophisticated feedback, or assigning lower grades and track recommendations-thereby perpetuating inequality <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bloem et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Brummelman et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Brummelman & Sedikides, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Turetsky et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we shift attention from overtly negative practices to a potentially overlooked source of inequality: praise, which is often intended to support students from disadvantaged backgrounds.
Indeed, teachers tend to praise students from disadvantaged backgrounds more often (Harber, 2023; Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023).
text.formatted: Indeed, teachers tend to praise students from disadvantaged backgrounds more often <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Harber, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We theorize that, in some cases, praise can backfire by communicating teachers' low expectations to children (Good et al., 2018; Graham & Chen, 2020).
text.formatted: We theorize that, in some cases, praise can backfire by communicating teachers' low expectations to children <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Good et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Graham & Chen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: According to attribution theory (Graham, 2020), people often assume success and failure are caused by internal factors like effort or ability.
text.formatted: According to attribution theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Graham, 2020)</ref>, people often assume success and failure are caused by internal factors like effort or ability.

text.text: Like most adults (Celniker et al., 2023), teachers value effort (Biddle & Goudas, 1997; Weiner & Kukla, 1970) and praise the students they believe worked hard (Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023; Weiner & Kukla, 1970).
text.formatted: Like most adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Celniker et al., 2023)</ref>, teachers value effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Biddle & Goudas, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Weiner & Kukla, 1970)</ref> and praise the students they believe worked hard <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Weiner & Kukla, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: For example, teachers give more praise to students who succeeded through effort than to those who succeeded effortlessly (Covington & Omelich, 1979b , 1979a).
text.formatted: For example, teachers give more praise to students who succeeded through effort than to those who succeeded effortlessly <ref type="bibr">(Covington & Omelich, 1979b</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 1979a)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, teachers give more rewards to students with low ability who succeeded through hard work than to students with high ability who succeeded effortlessly (Weiner & Kukla, 1970).
text.formatted: In fact, teachers give more rewards to students with low ability who succeeded through hard work than to students with high ability who succeeded effortlessly <ref type="bibr">(Weiner & Kukla, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: Children tend to understand that teachers praise those who succeed through effort.
From around age four, children infer that when a teacher praises one out of two students, the praised student worked harder-even if the praise makes no mention of effort (Barker & Graham, 1987).
text.formatted: From around age four, children infer that when a teacher praises one out of two students, the praised student worked harder-even if the praise makes no mention of effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barker & Graham, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Such unequal praise can communicate low ability.
When two students achieve the same success, the one who worked harder is often seen as lower in ability (Muenks & Miele, 2017).
text.formatted: When two students achieve the same success, the one who worked harder is often seen as lower in ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Muenks & Miele, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Children know that teachers praise for effort, so when they see that two students achieved the same success but only one student is praised by the teacher, they infer that the praised student is less smart (Barker & Graham, 1987; Miller & Hom Jr., 1996; Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023).
text.formatted: Children know that teachers praise for effort, so when they see that two students achieved the same success but only one student is praised by the teacher, they infer that the praised student is less smart <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barker & Graham, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Miller & Hom Jr., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, children use unequal praise as a low-ability cue when evaluating others.
Crucially, however, it is unknown whether children make these inferences about themselves.
When children achieve the same result as a classmate, but the teacher praises only them, would they infer that they themselves are less smart?
This is a critical question because praise that lowers children's self-perceived ability can contribute to achievement gaps (Brummelman & Sedikides, 2023; Hofer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is a critical question because praise that lowers children's self-perceived ability can contribute to achievement gaps <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Brummelman & Sedikides, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Hofer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: From what age may children infer from praise that they are less smart?

To make such an inference, children need to understand that those who succeed through hard work tend to be less smart than those who succeed effortlessly (i.e., the understanding that effort and ability can be compensatory).

Some research suggests that, while young children think that those who work harder are smarter, children from age 9-12 understand that those who have to work harder tend to be less smart (for overviews, see Barker & Graham, 1987; Muenks & Miele, 2017; Nicholls, 1978).
text.formatted: Some research suggests that, while young children think that those who work harder are smarter, children from age 9-12 understand that those who have to work harder tend to be less smart (for overviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Barker & Graham, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Muenks & Miele, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Nicholls, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, studies adopting a third-person perspective found that older children (from about age 11) inferred that a child who received more praise for the same achievement was more hardworking but less smart (Miller & Hom Jr., 1996).
text.formatted: Accordingly, studies adopting a third-person perspective found that older children (from about age 11) inferred that a child who received more praise for the same achievement was more hardworking but less smart <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Miller & Hom Jr., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, younger children inferred that the child who received more praise was more hardworking and smarter (Barker & Graham, 1987).
text.formatted: By contrast, younger children inferred that the child who received more praise was more hardworking and smarter <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barker & Graham, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: However, recent work suggests that even children from age four can perceive effort and ability as compensatory (Cimpian, 2017; Muradoglu & Cimpian, 2020).
text.formatted: However, recent work suggests that even children from age four can perceive effort and ability as compensatory <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cimpian, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Muradoglu & Cimpian, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, whether children use unequal praise as a cue for low ability likely depends on children's understanding that effort and ability can be compensatory.
This understanding likely develops before the age of 11, but whether children apply this understanding spontaneously may differ between contexts (Cimpian, 2017).
text.formatted: This understanding likely develops before the age of 11, but whether children apply this understanding spontaneously may differ between contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cimpian, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For this reason, we included a broad age range-children ages 7-13 years-so that we could explore age differences.
We evaluated these differences rigorously.
If children understand only from age 11 that effort and ability are compensatory, the effect of praise on self-perceived ability should be more pronounced for older children.

Moreover, it should be more pronounced for children with a fixed mindset (Dweck, 1999)-who believe that ability is fixed, which leads them to believe that working hard signals low ability-and those who explicitly endorse the belief that working hard signals low ability (Miller & Hom Jr., 1996; Muenks & Miele, 2017).
text.formatted: Moreover, it should be more pronounced for children with a fixed mindset <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dweck, 1999)</ref>-who believe that ability is fixed, which leads them to believe that working hard signals low ability-and those who explicitly endorse the belief that working hard signals low ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Miller & Hom Jr., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Muenks & Miele, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We explored all three possibilities.

To date, the impact of teacher praise on children's self-perceived abilities has not been investigated directly, probably because researchers lacked the tools to create a dynamic classroom setting where the causal impact of teacher praise can be studied experimentally.
Creating such a setting, where children complete tasks alongside a classmate while being observed by the teacher, is almost impossible in regular laboratory settings.
We therefore developed a novel Virtual Reality (VR) procedure to recreate this context in a virtual world.
VR combines the ecological validity of real-life interactions with the experimental control typically found in laboratory experiments (Blascovich et al., 2002).
text.formatted: VR combines the ecological validity of real-life interactions with the experimental control typically found in laboratory experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Blascovich et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Children are immersed, from a first-person perspective, in a standardized yet lifelike context, which elicits more intense social processing than vignette-based methods (Verhoef et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Children are immersed, from a first-person perspective, in a standardized yet lifelike context, which elicits more intense social processing than vignette-based methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Verhoef et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Children feel even more immersed in VR than adults do (Sharar et al., 2007), making it a particularly compelling tool for developmental research.
text.formatted: Children feel even more immersed in VR than adults do <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Sharar et al., 2007)</ref>, making it a particularly compelling tool for developmental research.

text.text: In the present research, we used VR to create the two necessary conditions under which praise can make children feel smart.
First, children completed tasks alongside a virtual classmate, achieved the same success, and then received praise or no praise from the teacher.
Only such a social-comparative context-where one person receives more praise than another-can lead praise to convey a message of low ability.

Second, while children completed the tasks, they were observed by the teacher, who appeared to be knowledgeable of their abilities: Teachers observed children solving practice tasks (Study 1) or said that they had received information from children's parents about children's abilities (Study 2).
Only when teachers appear knowledgeable of children's abilities can their praise signal low ability.
We conducted two preregistered experiments in this dynamic virtual classroom environment.
Children completed tasks alongside a virtual classmate while being observed by a virtual teacher who appeared knowledgeable about the children's prior abilities.
Children achieved the same score as their classmate.
In Study 1, the teacher praised the child or the classmate.
In Study 2, we added two control conditions, so that the teacher praised the child, the classmate, both, or neither.

Across both studies, we used general praise (e.g., "You did such a great job"), rather than effort praise (e.g., "You must have worked really hard"), as a critical test of the hypothesis that praise-even if it does not mention effort explicitly-signals to children that they are hardworking rather than smart.
We hypothesized that receiving praise, while an equally achieving classmate does not, would make children feel less smart.
In Study 2, we explored the effects of teacher praise on children's physiological arousal, capturing in-the-moment affective responses that children may be unable or unwilling to report.

If praise induces stress, it should increase heart rate, decrease heart rate variability, and increase skin conductance-responses which reflect parasympathetic withdrawal, a mix of sympathetic activation and parasympathetic withdrawal, and sympathetic activation, respectively (Kreibig, 2010).
text.formatted: If praise induces stress, it should increase heart rate, decrease heart rate variability, and increase skin conductance-responses which reflect parasympathetic withdrawal, a mix of sympathetic activation and parasympathetic withdrawal, and sympathetic activation, respectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Kreibig, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: If praise induces social-evaluative threat, it should lead to blushing, an involuntary reddening of the face that occurs in response to perceived social scrutiny or evaluation, when individuals are worried that others might form unfavorable impressions of them (Brummelman et al., 2018; Leary et al., 1992).
text.formatted: If praise induces social-evaluative threat, it should lead to blushing, an involuntary reddening of the face that occurs in response to perceived social scrutiny or evaluation, when individuals are worried that others might form unfavorable impressions of them <ref type="bibr">(Brummelman et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Leary et al., 1992)</ref>.

text.text: We hypothesized that children who received praise from the teacher while an equally performing classmate did not (self-praise condition) would perceive themselves as less smart (H1) and more hardworking (H2) than children who did not receive praise while their classmate did (other-praise condition).

We explored whether praise influenced how children believe the teacher viewed their effort and ability, how liked children felt by the teacher, and how many challenges children took on (as low self-perceived ability may reduce challenge seeking, Zhao & Hu, 2026).
text.formatted: We explored whether praise influenced how children believe the teacher viewed their effort and ability, how liked children felt by the teacher, and how many challenges children took on (as low self-perceived ability may reduce challenge seeking, Zhao & Hu, 2026).

text.text: We also explored whether effects of praise were moderated by task achievement and perceived task difficulty.
Participants were 237 children from Dutch elementary schools.
We excluded 25 children who met preregistered exclusion criteria: fully missing data on key dependent variables (n = 22), incorrect praise delivery (n = 2), or technical malfunctions (n = 1).
The final sample contained 212 children (59% girls, 41% boys, < 1% another gender, age: 7-12, M = 9.72, SD = 1.14).
text.formatted: The final sample contained 212 children (59% girls, 41% boys, < 1% another gender, age: 7-12, M = 9.72, SD = 1.14).

text.text: Most participants (96%) were born in the Netherlands (see Supplemental Material for details on socioeconomic background).
We received active informed parental consent for children's participation, and children provided assent.
Experimenters first visited schools to administer baseline surveys.
Children reported their mindset by responding to the six items from the Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scale for Children (Dweck, 1999).
text.formatted: Children reported their mindset by responding to the six items from the Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scale for Children <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dweck, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Example items include: "You have a certain amount of intelligence, and you can't really do much to change it" (0 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree).
Fixed-mindset items were reverse-coded, so higher scores indicated a stronger growth mindset (α = .82, M = 2.74, SD = 1.05).
Experimenters then visited schools to conduct VR sessions with each child individually.
Children wore a head-mounted display creating a multisensory environment, making it feel as though they had stepped into a generated world (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Children wore a head-mounted display creating a multisensory environment, making it feel as though they had stepped into a generated world (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Before children entered the virtual classroom, the experimenter told them that a real teacher and child from other schools were participating simultaneously (in reality, they were controlled by the experimenter).
In the virtual classroom, children and the virtual classmate completed five puzzles each (called "figure-test"), alternating turns, with the participants going first.
The teacher told the students that the puzzles in each round were equally difficult.
The puzzles, displayed on the board, were Raven matrices consisting of nine-piece patterns with the last piece missing, alongside eight numbered options for the missing piece (Raven, 1989).
text.formatted: The puzzles, displayed on the board, were Raven matrices consisting of nine-piece patterns with the last piece missing, alongside eight numbered options for the missing piece <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Raven, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Children picked an answer for each puzzle and said their answer out loud.
To create the impression that the teacher had some knowledge of the students' abilities, children completed a practice round of three puzzles before solving the five main tasks.
After completing all puzzles, the teacher told the children that they had both received the same score (three out of five), regardless of how the participating child had actually performed.
Children were then randomly assigned to one of the two conditions.
In the self-praise condition, the child was praised, but the virtual classmate was not.
In the other-praise condition, the virtual classmate was praised, but the child was not.
The teacher walked to the non-praised child first (ensuring participants noticed that the other child had not been praised) and said: "[Name], you got three out of five puzzles right."
The teacher then walked to the praised child and said: "[Name], you got three out of five puzzles right.
Wow, you did such a great job!
Honestly, that's really impressive!"
After exiting the virtual environment, we measured our preregistered outcomes (via a survey on a tablet): self-perceived ability and effort (in randomized order).
Children were asked: "Who is smarter, do you think?
You or the other student?"
and then "How much smarter are you/is the other student, do you think?"
(a bit, quite a bit, much smarter).
An overall score was created, ranging from0 = the classmate is much smarter than I am; to5 = I am much smarter than the classmate (selfperceived ability, M = 2.65, SD = 0.82).
Children were also asked: "Who worked harder on the task, do you think?
You or the other student?"
and "How much harder did you/the other student work, do you think?"
An overall score was created, ranging from0 = the classmate worked much harder than I did; to5 = I worked much harder than the classmate (self-perceived effort, M = 2.75, SD = 0.78).
To index exploratory outcomes, children returned to the virtual classroom.

To measure challenge seeking, they chose four times whether they wanted to do an easy task (with low chances of making mistakes, from which they would not learn much; scored 0) or a difficult task (with higher chances of making mistakes, from which they could learn a lot; scored 1).
We created a mean score reflecting challenge seeking (M = .55, SD = .26).
After children exited the virtual classroom, we measured perceived teacher view of own ability, perceived teacher view of own effort, and perceived teacher liking (in randomized order, 6point scale).
Children were asked: "Who does the teacher think is smarter, do you think?
You or the other student?"
and "How much smarter does the teacher think you are/the other student is, do you think?"
(M = 2.66, SD = 0.85); "Who does the teacher think worked harder on the task, do you think?
You or the other student?"
and "How much harder does the teacher think you/the other student worked?"
(M = 2.75, SD = 0.77); and "Who does the teacher like better, do you think?
You or the other student?"
and "How much more does the teacher like you/the other student?"
Children were prompted to think back to when the teacher told them what score they got and were asked whom the teacher gave a compliment then (only them or only the other student).
Children were asked: "What did you think of the VR?"
They responded to the items "It just felt real" and "I was totally immersed in it" (0 = not true at all to3 = completely true, Verhoef et al., 2022).
text.formatted: They responded to the items "It just felt real" and "I was totally immersed in it" (0 = not true at all to3 = completely true, <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Verhoef et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We created a mean score (r = .39).
Children were asked how many puzzles (0-5) they thought they had gotten right before the teacher had told them their score (M = 3.26, SD = 1.00).
We coded children's task performance based on screen and audio recordings (valid data was available for 192 out of 212 children as some screen-recordings were missing, M = 2.49, SD = 0.93).
Children were also asked: "How difficult did you find the figure-test?"
(0 = not difficult at all to3 = really difficult, M = 1.33, SD = 0.55).

We ran six linear regression models (i.e., one for each dependent variable) to determine the effect of condition (dichotomous; self-praise, scored as -1 vs. other-praise, scored as 1) on preregistered outcomes self-perceived ability and effort, and on exploratory outcomes challenge seeking, perceived teacher view of own ability and effort, and perceived teacher liking.
We conducted analyses in R version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2023) using the lm.beta package (Behrendt, 2023).
text.formatted: We conducted analyses in R version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2023) using the lm.beta package <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Behrendt, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We used the University of Amsterdam's developed artificial intelligence website to refine our data analysis code.
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study.

text.text: Contrary to our hypotheses, we found no evidence that receiving unequal praise made children feel less smart or more hardworking than their classmate.
We also found no evidence that it led children to think that the teacher found them less smart, more hardworking, or liked them more than their classmate.
Moreover, we found no evidence that any potential praise effects differed depending on children's age or mindset.
In Study 2, we sought to establish, with greater confidence, that receiving praise does not make children feel less smart.
To do so, we improved our design.

First, we added control conditions in which neither child or both children received praise, so as to rule out that effects can be explained by receiving any praise at all instead of receiving more praise than a fellow student.
Second, we made the praise more salient by having children solve tasks and receiving praise twice (rather than just once).
Third, we measured physiological arousal to capture immediate responses related to stress and social-evaluative threat that children may be unwilling to report.
We also improved our outcome measures.

First, we measured absolute rather than comparative self-judgements (e.g., "I am good at this" rather than "I am better at this than the other student") because the added control conditions in which both the child and the classmate were praised made social comparisons less meaningful.
Second, we measured task-specific rather than domain-general self-perceived ability and effort because task-specific beliefs may shift more easily.

Third, we measured task-elicited rather than self-initiated effort ("I had to work hard" rather than "I worked hard") because task-elicited effort is typically interpreted as compensating for low ability (Muenks & Miele, 2017).

text.text: Fourth, we measured interest in activities for "smart" vs. "hardworking" children (Bian et al., 2017) instead of challenge seeking to provide additional evidence that praise does not affect motivational outcomes.

text.text: Fifth, we measured state self-esteem to capture whether praise makes children feel less worthy.
Sixth, we measured children's understanding of effort and ability as compensatory to investigate whether praise effects depend on this understanding.

We hypothesized that children who received praise while their classmate did not (self-praise condition) would report lower perceived teacher view of own ability (H1), self-perceived ability (H2), and state self-esteem (H3) than children who did not receive praise while their classmate did (otherpraise condition).
We explored comparisons with conditions in which both children were praised (both-praise condition) or neither child was praised (neither-praise condition).
We explored whether praise influenced self-perceived effort, perceived teacher liking, interest in activities for "smart" vs.
"hardworking" children, and physiological arousal.
We tested whether effects of condition on outcomes were moderated by task achievement and perceived task difficulty.
Participants were 257 children.
Participants visited Science Center NEMO, a Dutch science museum in Amsterdam.
The research was part of Science Live, a program that enables scientists to use NEMO visitors as participants.

We excluded 32 participants who met preregistered exclusion criteria: the parent/caregiver withdrew consent (n = 1), fully missing data on key dependent variables (n = 21), incorrect praise delivery (n = 3), technical malfunctions (n = 2), or pilot sessions (n = 6).
The final sample contained 225 children (48% girls, 51% boys, 1% another gender), aged 8-13 (M = 10.12 years, SD = 1.58).
Most participants (97%) were born in the Netherlands (see Supplemental Material for details on socioeconomic background).
We received active informed parental consent for children's participation and children provided assent.
Participating children first filled in a baseline survey.
We used the same measures as in Study 1 for mindset (α = .78, M = 3.12, SD = 0.93).

Children reported their perceived relationship between effort and ability by responding to four items, such as: "If you have to work very hard to achieve something, you are probably not very smart" (0 = not true at all to3 = completely true).
The four items ( = .76) were averaged to create a mean score, with higher values indicating a stronger belief in a compensatory relationship between effort and ability (M = 0.98, SD = 0.63).
Participanting children then took part in the VR sessions.

Children solved tasks (called "Memory," remembering as many objects as possible out of a set of objects displayed for 20 seconds) along with a virtual classmate in a virtual classroom, were told their score, and that the virtual classmate had the same score by a virtual teacher, and received (or did not receive) praise.
Solving the tasks and receiving praise occurred twice (trial 1 and 2).

To create the impression that the teacher had some knowledge of the students' abilities, in the beginning of the VR session, the teacher appeared to review information about the students' abilities supposedly provided by parents/caregivers.
After exiting the virtual environment, we measured preregistered outcomes (in randomized order).
Children were asked: "How good are you at memory, according to [name teacher]?
[Name teacher] probably thinks…".
They responded to the items "that I am good at Memory", "that I can do Memory well", and "that I have talent for Memory" (0 = not true at all to3 = completely true; α = .85).
We created a mean score (M = 1.79, SD = 0.64).
Children were also asked: "How good are you at Memory, do you think?
In this moment, I think…".
They responded to the same items as for the measure of teacher-perceived view of own ability.
We created a mean score (α = .84; M = 1.69, SD = 0.65).
Children also responded to a shortened version of the State Self-Esteem scale (Thomaes et al., 2010).

We then measured exploratory outcomes.

We created a mean score (α = .82, M = 2.09, SD = 0.70).

We preregistered analyses involving the two critical conditions: the self-praise and otherpraise conditions.

We ran ANOVAs for the preregistered outcomes perceived teacher view of own ability, self-perceived ability, and state self-esteem, and for exploratory outcomes self-perceived effort and perceived teacher liking to determine the effect of condition on the outcomes.

As preregistered, our interest was in specific pairwise comparisons between the self-praise and otherpraise condition, rather than in the overall omnibus F-tests, so we focused on Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons between these two conditions.
For exploratory outcome game interest, ratings were nested within participants.

We thus ran a mixed-effects model predicting game interest from game type (dummy coded using smart game as reference category), experimental condition (dummy coded using self-praise condition as reference category), and their interaction, with a random intercept for participants.
We re-ran the model using the other-praise condition as the reference condition.

For exploratory outcomes physiological arousal, we ran mixed-effects models predicting heart rate, blushing, and skin conductance from experimental condition (dummy coded using selfpraise as the reference condition), period (recall = 1, praise = 0), trial (trial1 = 0, trial2 = 1), and baseline physiology (grand-mean-centered), the interactions between period and the condition dummies, and between period and trial, with a random intercept for participants.

We ran a mixedeffects model predicting heart rate variability from experimental condition, trial, baseline HRV (grand-mean-centered), and the interaction between the conditions and trial, with a random intercept for participants.

The effect of condition on self-and teacher-perceived ability, state self-esteem, self-perceived effort, perceived teacher liking, game interest, and physiological arousal was not significantly moderated by age, mindset, or perceived relationship between effort and ability, and was also not significantly moderated by task performance, perceived task difficulty, or immersion in the virtual environment (there were some unexpected significant condition effects, but these effects were not consistent across measures; see Supplemental Material).
Contrary to our preregistered hypotheses, we found no evidence that unequal praise made children feel less smart, experience lower state self-esteem, or think the teacher found them less smart.
We also found no evidence that it led children to feel more hardworking, show a stronger preference for games for "hardworking" (rather than "smart") children, or have higher physiological arousal.
Moreover, we found no evidence that any potential praise effects differed depending on children's age, mindset, or perceived relationship between effort and ability.
Children thought that teachers liked praised students.
This finding likely emerged only in Study 2 because the praise was more salient, and our updated measure picked up on more nuanced changes in perceived liking.

We used a novel Virtual Reality paradigm to test a previously unexamined question: Does receiving praise from the teacher-while an equally performing classmate is not praised-make children feel less smart?

Across two highly powered and preregistered VR experiments in which we recreated a naturalistic classroom context and effectively manipulated teacher praise, we found no evidence that praise made children feel less smart.
We also found no evidence that it raised children's physiological arousal, suggesting that praise did not trigger feelings that children were unwilling or unable to report.
These results cast doubt on the widely held belief that teacher praise can make children feel less smart.
Our findings suggest a dissociation between how praise makes children think about others versus the self.

Previous research has adopted a third-person perspective, showing that when children learn that two students achieved the same outcome but only one of them was praised, they infer that the praised student is more hardworking but less smart (Barker & Graham, 1987; Miller & Hom Jr., 1996; Schoneveld & Brummelman, 2023).

text.text: Using VR, we adopted a first-person perspective, finding no evidence that when children achieve the same outcome as a classmate but only they themselves are praised, they feel more hardworking or less smart.
Thus, teacher praise can make children seem less smart in the eyes of others, but not necessarily in their own eyes.
Why may teacher praise not make children feel less smart?
Children may evaluate themselves and others through two basic dimensions-warmth and competence (Fiske et al., 2007).

text.text: We suggest that when children meet a new teacher, they care primarily about being liked, less about being seen as smart, as establishing a positive relationship may matter most in such situations (Madjar et al., 2018; Urdan & Maehr, 1995).

text.text: Indeed, in interpersonal encounters, individuals tend to initially focus on warmth before evaluating competence (Fiske et al., 2007).

text.text: This may be particularly true for children in elementary school who have to navigate new social environments (Eskelä-Haapanen et al., 2017; van Rens et al., 2019).

text.text: Our findings concur: Study 2 suggests that children view praise as a sign of being liked by the teacher.
In particular, children who were praised by the teacher inferred that the teacher liked them more and liked the classmate less.
Did teacher praise make only some children feel less smart?

One possibility is that teacher praise made only children from low socioeconomic status backgrounds feel less smart, because they may be attuned to low-ability cues due to frequent stigmatization (e.g., Goudeau et al., 2025).

text.text: Challenging this possibility, exploratory analyses revealed that the effects of teacher praise were not moderated by students' objective or subjective socioeconomic status (see Supplemental Material).
Another possibility is that teacher praise made only those children feel less smart who believe that those who work hard are less smart.

This should be most true for older children, children who see an inverse relation between effort and ability, and children with a fixed mindset-groups who tend to infer that those who work hard are less smart (Cimpian, 2017; Dweck, 1999; Muenks & Miele, 2017).

The effects of praise did not differ between younger and older children.

Regardless of their age, children thus may not interpret unequal praise they experience from a first-person perspective as a low-ability cue.

Our research pioneered Virtual Reality for testing causal effects of teacher praise in a classroom setting, combined self-reports with physiological measures, and replicated findings across two well-powered experiments with control conditions and moderators.
Our study also has limitations, which offer new research directions.

First, our VR experiment does not capture teacher-student interactions as they unfold over weeks, months, or even years (Asaba, Santos, et al., 2025; Asaba, Stegall, et al., 2025; Corriveau & Harris, 2009).

text.text: Future research should capture exactly when and how teacher praise can become a low-ability cue in teacher-student dyads.
Second, we investigated effects of general praise.

text.text: If applicable, parents also reported education, country of birth, occupation, and income for the child's other parent or caregiver.
To include objective socioeconomic status (SES) as a moderator for our analyses, we computed aggregate objective SES scores.
In Study 1, we only included parental education.
When educational levels of both parents were available, we averaged them.
If only the educational level of one parent was available, we used only that value.
In Study 2, we included parental education, income, and occupation.

When education and occupational prestige levels of both parents was available, we averaged them across parents; when only the education and/or occupational prestige level of one parent was available, we used only that value.
When income levels of both parents are available, we added up the incomes of both parents; when only income of one parent was available, we used only that value.
There were no univariate outliers for education or occupation.
For household income (sum of both parents' incomes), four participants had univariate outliers (18749; 20249.5; 22249.5; and 30499.5).
We winsorized these outliers by transforming them to the value at the 95t percentile of the data (12999).

Finally, we z-transformed (i.e., standardized) the values for family-level education, occupation, and income, averaged them (Cronbach  = .76), and z-scored the average to create the aggregate objective SES index (range = -2.67 -2.21, M = 0.00, SD = 1.00).

For Study 2, we examined whether the effect of condition on teacher-perceived ability, selfperceived ability, state self-esteem, perceived teacher liking, and physiological arousal was moderated by individual or contextual factors.

We conducted regression models in which we included a) theoretical moderators (i.e., subjective SES, objective SES, age, mindset, perceived relationship between effort and ability, objective task performance, perceived task difficulty) and b) a methodological moderator (immersion in the virtual environment).

For each outcome, both preregistered and exploratory, we tested regression models including condition (dummy-coded with self-praise as the reference group), the moderator, and their interaction as predictors.
Moderators were mean-centered; subjective SES was not additionally centered because it was z-standardized prior to analysis.
While SSS, task performance and immersion showed significant interactions with some condition dummies (see Table S5.2), none of these interaction effects were consistent across all conditions.

text.text: We also examined whether the effect of condition on game interest (interest in a game for smart vs. hardworking children) was moderated by individual or contextual factors.

We estimated linear mixed-effects models predicting game interest from game type (smart game as the reference category), experimental condition (self-praise as the reference category), the mean-centered moderator, and their three-way interaction, with a random intercept for participants to account for the repeated-measures structure of the data.

We tested moderation using the omnibus Type III Ftest of the three-way interaction, which tests whether the interaction between game type, condition, and the moderator differs from zero across all condition contrasts jointly.
None of these three-way interactions became significant.

We processed the physiological data using the start marker of each period.
HRV data was sampled in 30-second segments following the guideline for HRV studies (Quigley et al., 2024), and all other physiological measures were sampled every 2 seconds.

text.text: Following baseline markers, we extracted an average over 60 second-period of data for all measures; following recall-and praisemarkers, we extracted 30 seconds of data for HRV (as this is a recommended minimum), and 20 seconds for the other measures (since the marker type with the shortest average duration was 20 seconds, and using this window ensured consistency across participants).

If a participant's period (calculated based on the time difference between the start and end markers placed during the experiment) lasted less than 10 seconds, we excluded all physiological data for that period.

If a participant's period lasted between 10 and 20 seconds, we excluded HRV values (as HRV requires a minimum of 30 seconds to yield reliable estimates), and computed the mean for the remaining physiological measures using only the markers that fit within the actual duration.

text.text: To account for individual differences in physiological reactivity, we included a random intercept for each child, but did not estimate random slopes to avoid convergence issues.

The main effect of period reflects the difference in physiological arousal between the recall and praise phases within the reference condition during trial 1; The main effects of the condition dummy variables represent differences in physiological arousal during the praise phase of trial 1 between each experimental condition and the reference group; the period with condition interactions indicate whether the change in arousal from recall to praise (i.e., physiological reactivity) differs between each condition and the self-praise condition; The period with trial interaction tests whether the magnitude or direction of physiological reactivity differs between the two trials.
We ran an extended model including the condition with trial and period with condition with trial (three-way) interactions.
For none of the physiological measures did these interaction terms become significant, indicating that the effects of condition and period were consistent across the two trials.
To follow up significant period with condition interactions, we used estimated marginal means derived from a model in which condition was specified as a four-level factor.

We fit a simpler linear mixed-effects model for the exploratory outcome heart rate variability (to account for the high number of missing values on the recall-periods), in which we only compared arousal differences during praise between the different conditions while controlling for baseline.
We included predictors experimental condition, trial, baseline HRV (grand-mean-centered, covariate), and the interaction between the conditions and trial.
We also included a random intercept for participant.
Our primary interest was in specific pairwise comparisons, rather than in the overall omnibus F-tests, so we focused on pairwise comparisons.
To compare all conditions, we estimated all models with other reference groups too.
The main effects of the condition dummy variables represent differences in HRV during the praise phase of trial 1 between each experimental condition and the reference condition.
The condition with trial interactions indicate whether the pattern of HRV change from trial 1 to trial 2 differed between each condition and the self-praise condition.

text.text: Children in the self-praise condition did not differ from those in the neither-praise condition in terms of their heart rate.

This suggests that when children receive more praise than an equally achieving classmate, their heart rate shows a smaller decrease after solving the task than when they receive equal praise as a classmate.

For Study 1, we examined whether the effect of condition on preregistered outcomes (selfperceived ability and effort) and exploratory outcomes (teacher-perceived ability and effort, perceived teacher liking, and challenge seeking) was moderated by individual or contextual factors.

We conducted regression models in which we included a) theoretical moderators (i.e., objective and subjective socioeconomic status, age, mindset, perceived and objective task performance, perceived task difficulty) and b) a methodological moderator (immersion in the virtual environment).
For each outcome, both preregistered and exploratory, we tested regression models including condition, the mean-centered moderator, and their interaction as predictors.
All continuous moderators were mean-centered prior to analysis.

text.text: Electrocardiography (ECG) was recorded using a three-electrode bipolar configuration.
Two active 3M Red Dot electrodes were placed on the left and right upper chest (below the clavicles), and a ground electrode was placed on the upper back.

The ECG signal was sampled at 1,000 Hz and filtered using second-order high-pass (0.2 Hz) and fourth-order low-pass (75 Hz) Butterworth filters, with an additional 50 Hz notch filter to remove mains interference.
Rpeaks were automatically detected using VSRRP9's built-in absolute-value peak detection algorithm.
A dynamically adjusting window of valid inter-beat intervals (IBIs) was applied to identify physiologically plausible beats when calculating heart rate and HRV.
From the ECG, heart rate (HR; beats per minute) and heart rate variability (HRV) were extracted.
HRV was quantified as the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD; ms) over 30-s epochs.

Blushing was recorded with a dual-wavelength reflective photoplethysmograph (red) The sensor was fastened on the skin of one cheekbone, low enough so that the VR goggles, which were placed first, did not press on it.
Photoplethysmograph signals were sampled at 1000 Hz in plethysmography mode and band-pass filtered with a high-pass filter at 0.2 Hz (2nd order) and a low-pass filter at 5 Hz (4th order).
Blushing was indexed from plethysmograph amplitude (red), reflecting changes in facial blood volume at the cheekbone.
PLETH amplitudes were derived from the largest peak-to-trough value in each window, where the window size was defined based on the inter-beat interval.
Skin conductance level (SCL) was recorded using Ag/AgCl electrodes, sampled at 1000 Hz, and low-pass filtered at 10 Hz (4th order).
Electrodes were attached to the index and middle fingers of the left hand with medical tape.
The SCL signal was expressed in microsiemens (µS).
All filters were implemented as digital Butterworth filters.
No artifact correction was applied to ECG, blushing, measure, by computing z-scores across participants).
For each period, we calculated how many values should be present based on its duration (1 value every 2 seconds).
If the number of remaining non-missing values was less than half of this expected number, all values from that period were removed.

Second, we removed all markers belonging to a given period if no (i.e., all markers across a period had the same value) or almost no (i.e., only two unique values were present across a period) within-period variation was present in that period, if extreme jumps (changes between successive values that exceeded the individual's mean difference ± 4 standard deviations) were present in that period for heart rate and skin conductance.
